design_detail: Mixed-methods online survey (Qualtrics), pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/35kbs) and approved by the University of Bristol School of Psychological Science ethics committee (116995). Quantitative part (rated with ROBINS-E): 163 adults with at least two lifetime uses of a classic psychedelic or an analogue, recruited through university societies and online psychedelic communities, each recalled, in one sitting, their first and their most recent psychedelic experience outside research or therapy and above a microdose: time since, substance, place, intention, which listed harm-reduction practices they used (before, during, during 'myths', after), the Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ; 24 of its 26 items asked) and the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (EBI). They then rated each practice's importance for a safe experience from −10 to +10. A practice's Harm Reduction Score is its mean importance rating in the sample; a person's Participant Harm Reduction Score for an occasion is the sum of the Harm Reduction Scores of the practices they reported using then. Analyses: repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t test (first versus most recent), Pearson correlations of the score with CEQ and EBI, and an unplanned descriptive comparison of party settings with other settings. Qualitative part (described, not rated): inductive three-stage thematic analysis of 61 free-text comments, mainly by the senior author with the first author.
can_establish: Which places, intentions and listed practices 163 self-selected, mostly male, experienced people who use psychedelics recalled for their first and most recent experiences, how they rated the importance of each practice for safety, and whether people who recalled using more practices rated as important also recalled more emotional breakthrough and, for the first experience, fewer challenging experiences.
cannot_establish: Whether any practice prevents challenging experiences or brings about emotional breakthrough (retrospective, unadjusted correlations of about 0.2 between ratings made at one sitting, with the predictor weighted by the same respondents' importance judgments and including practices after the experience); whether people adopt more harm reduction as they gain experience (a first experience recalled a median 42 months later is compared with a recent one recalled after a median 2 months, among people who kept using); or how common any practice is among people who use psychedelics generally.

sample.recruitment: Opportunistic: advertisements through relevant university societies and online psychedelic communities led to the Qualtrics survey; an optional link allowed entry to a prize draw for a £50 voucher (Methods › Participants; Procedure).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over; at least two lifetime uses of a classic psychedelic (LSD, psilocybin, DMT, mescaline) or an analogue or derivative (for example 2C-B); fluent in English. Neither the first nor the most recent experience could have been in a research study or a professional therapy setting, or a microdose (self-defined; no definition was given). Three attention checks; many respondents were excluded for failing them (numbers and details in the supplement, not read).
sample.demographics: Mean age 27.5 (SD 8.06), median 26, mode 20, range 18 to 56; 13 aged 40 or over; 120 men, 35 women, 8 non-binary. Estimated lifetime psychedelic uses: mean 28.4 (SD 45.2), median 11.5, mode 20, with 16 people estimating 100 to 300 uses. Education and the substances ever used are in supplementary Table S1 (not read).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). The number who started, the number excluded and item non-response are given only in the supplement (not read); every analysis uses 163.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected through university societies and psychedelic communities and largely male. Requiring two or more lifetime uses excludes people who stopped after their first experience; the authors note possible survivor bias towards people with fewer unpleasant early experiences and a lower propensity to harm (Discussion › Strengths, limitations and future directions, 2nd paragraph). The first-versus-recent comparison is therefore made only among people who continued to use psychedelics.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported checklist of harm-reduction practices for each recalled experience, compiled by the authors from trusted online harm-reduction resources, the published literature and discussion with colleagues (the list and its sources are in supplementary Table S3, not read), grouped as before, during, during 'myths' (anecdotal beliefs and practices generally advised against for inexperienced people, such as being alone in a dark place, included partly to make respondents read the list carefully) and after. Importance for a safe experience was rated once for every practice, after both experiences had been reported, from −10 (detrimental) through 0 (no effect on safety) to +10 (extremely helpful). The Participant Harm Reduction Score sums the sample-mean importance of the practices a person used, so it mixes how many practices were used with how important the sample judged them. One practice, arranging a time to take the dose, had no importance scores because of a methodological error.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured for either experience: no amount, route or redosing record (the authors suggest that people using for the first time may have taken smaller amounts; Discussion › Strengths, limitations and future directions, 4th paragraph). Substance on the first and most recent occasion: LSD 47% and 33%, psilocybin 41% and 36%, 2C-B 4% and 6%, DMT 2% and 6%, mescaline 1% and 1%, other 6% and 18% (Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Some participants reported using other psychedelics or non-psychedelic drugs on the same occasion (Results › Characteristics of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph); not quantified in the main text or analysed. Smoking cannabis was one of the listed 'myth' practices; the authors call its effects equivocal.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (retrospective survey). Time since the first experience: mean 67.52 months (SD 78.33), median 42, mode 24; since the most recent: mean 8.68 months (SD 20.76), median 2, mode 1 (Table 1).

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant's first versus most recent experience. For the correlations, people with higher versus lower Participant Harm Reduction Scores. For setting, experiences at a party, club or festival (24 first, 12 most recent) versus all other places, descriptively only.
comparison.matching: None; no covariates in any analysis.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mental health, personality and amount taken were not measured; substance, place and intention were measured but not used as covariates, nor were the number of earlier experiences at the time of the most recent one or the time since each experience. Intentions changed strongly between occasions (curiosity 72% to 20%; spiritual pursuits 20% to 46%; processing difficult emotions 9% to 32%), and the authors themselves suggest intention and amount may explain differences between the experiences.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not measured beyond the mention of polydrug use on some occasions.

outcomes.instruments: CEQ (Barrett et al., 2016): seven subscales (isolation, grief, physical distress, fear, insanity, paranoia, death), items rated 0 to 5; 2 of the 3 insanity items were not asked because of an experimenter error, so 24 items were used; subscale scores are item means expressed as a percentage of the maximum; Cronbach's alpha 0.96 (first) and 0.95 (most recent). EBI (Roseman et al., 2019): six statements rated 0 to 100; alpha 0.92 and 0.93. Both were rated by the participant for each recalled experience, in the same sitting as the practice checklist.
outcomes.validity_norms: Both are validated questionnaires developed from internet surveys of people who used psychedelics. The shortened CEQ was not re-validated; the authors report internal consistency and an overall mean (17) similar to earlier studies. Neither has been validated for recall years after the experience.
outcomes.operationalization: A positive experience is a higher EBI score and a negative one a higher CEQ score, which the authors call proxies; they note that challenging experiences are not always negative and may precede breakthrough, and the two scores correlated positively (r = 0.39 first, 0.37 most recent). Harm itself (injury, need for help, lasting difficulties) was not measured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni for the post hoc comparisons after the ANOVA only. 15 counts the inferential tests printed in Results (3 ANOVA effects, 4 reported Bonferroni contrasts, the CEQ subscale ANOVA, the EBI paired t test, 2 EBI–CEQ correlations and 4 correlations of the Participant Harm Reduction Score with EBI and CEQ); 5 of them test the pre-registered hypotheses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: every measure is a self-rating by a participant who knew which practices they had reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Participant Harm Reduction Score, mean (SD): first 40.06 (18.90), most recent 48.68 (18.81); main effect of occasion F(1,162) = 28.32, p < 0.001 (printed partial eta squared 0.012; 0.15 from the F and df, editors' calculation). Bonferroni contrasts, most recent higher: before-use practices t = −9.63, p < 0.001; after-use t = −3.28, p = 0.03; during t = −1.47, p = 1; during-myths t = −0.04, p = 1. EBI: first 27.77 (26.46), most recent 39.18 (29.91), t(162) = 4.42, p < 0.001, d = 0.35 (equal to t divided by the square root of n, a paired dz; 0.40 when the difference is divided by the average SD, editors' calculation). CEQ: 17.14 (18.06) and 17.29 (17.06), no meaningful difference in any subscale. Correlations of the Participant Harm Reduction Score (n = 163; 95% CIs by Fisher z, editors' calculation): with EBI r = 0.24 on both occasions (0.09 to 0.38), p = 0.002; with CEQ, first experience r = −0.21 (−0.35 to −0.06), p = 0.006; most recent r = −0.15 (−0.30 to 0.00), p = 0.061. Shared variance 2% to 6% (editors' calculation).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Pre-registered on OSF (https://osf.io/35kbs/; DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/35KBS). The authors say they followed the registered analysis plan and flag the exploratory analyses (the EBI–CEQ correlation; the party-setting comparison, described as unplanned). Measurement deviations: 2 of the 3 CEQ insanity items were not asked, and one practice had no importance scores. The registration itself was not read for this card.
analysis.selective_reporting: The prevalence and importance score of each practice appear only in Figure 1 (an image that could not be viewed in this reading) and supplementary Table S3 (not read); the text describes only some practices. Four of the possible post hoc contrasts are reported. The abstract does not say that the CEQ correlation for the most recent experience was not statistically significant, or that the score includes practices used after the experience.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation is reported. Editors' calculation: 163 people give 80% power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect a correlation of about 0.22, so the most recent CEQ correlation (−0.15) could not be expected to reach significance; the authors call the party-setting analyses underpowered and ran no tests on them.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 163 self-selected experienced people who use psychedelics, recalling a first experience a median of three and a half years earlier and a recent one a median of two months earlier, the importance-weighted sum of practices used was higher for the recent experience, for practices before and after use but not during it. EBI was higher for the recent experience and CEQ was the same. The weighted practice score correlated weakly with EBI (r = 0.24 on both occasions) and with lower CEQ for the first experience (r = −0.21) but not significantly for the recent one (r = −0.15, p = 0.061). Experiences in party settings (24 first, 12 recent) had lower practice scores and higher CEQ, descriptively and untested; EBI was lower in party settings for the first experience only.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion reads the correlations as "some preliminary evidence that harm reduction practices may reduce negative and enhance positive experiences" (Discussion, 2nd paragraph) and as lending credibility to the importance ratings, although the score is built from those same ratings. The abstract and conclusion say the research helps to understand how engagement in harm reduction may increase with experience, a reading that rests on a recalled within-person comparison spanning years, with no allowance for recall, intention or amount. The abstract describes the CEQ association as strongest for the first experience rather than absent for the most recent one. The limitations paragraph says party settings were associated with lower EBI, which Table 2 shows only for the first experience (most recent: 41.56 in party settings versus 39.00 elsewhere), with no test run. Against this, the wording is hedged throughout, and the authors name survivor bias, forgetting, the missing CEQ items and the underpowered setting analysis.

timeline.event: Carbonaro et al. survey of the most difficult experience with psilocybin mushrooms, and Barrett et al.'s Challenging Experience Questionnaire, used here as background and measure (as cited).
Carhart-Harris et al. on the importance of context, cited for the dependence of psychedelic effects on set and setting
Haijen et al. prospective study, cited as earlier evidence that intentions, setting and readiness to confront difficult emotions predict CEQ and EBI scores
Roseman et al. validate the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory used here (as cited).
Gashi et al. interviews with experienced people who use psychedelics on turning bad trips into valuable experiences (as cited).
Simonsson et al. quota-stratified US survey: respondents linked their most challenging experience to no preparation, a negative mindset or no psychological support, also by retrospective self-report
Piercey et al. mini review cites this survey as the main outcome evidence for protective strategies with classical psychedelics and misstates parts of it (see that card)
Wood, McAlpine and Kamboj mixed-methods study of strategies for resolving challenging experiences, also retrospective

replication.where_it_stands: No replication with this list and score. Later studies on the same question (Simonsson et al., 2023; Wood et al., 2024) are also retrospective self-report, and a validated protective-strategies scale (Mian et al., 2023, as cited by Piercey et al., 2024) had not yet been tested against challenging experiences. Whether practices measured before use change the experience has not been tested prospectively.

funding.funder: As printed: Personal budget has been awarded to OMM by the School of Psychological Science at the University of Bristol (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: The authors declare no competing interests (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors from the School of Psychological Science, University of Bristol; the senior author also from the MRC Integrative Epidemiology Unit, University of Bristol. Data are openly available from the University of Bristol research data repository (data.bris, DOI 10.5523/bris.1r9y0tup0moyd2u03hy7jfjlgz).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people planning a psychedelic experience outside research or therapy that records planned practices, intentions, place and company beforehand, then the practices actually used and the amount, and the CEQ and EBI within days, analysing practices one by one rather than as an importance-weighted sum, with adjustment for prior experience, intention and amount, and with any importance ratings taken from an independent panel.

domains.note: No covariates at all. Intention (which shifted sharply between occasions), amount, substance, place, prior experience and mental health could each drive both the practices recalled and the CEQ and EBI ratings.

Recalled checklist (first experience a median of 42 months earlier) of an unvalidated list, weighted by importance ratings given by the same respondents after recalling both experiences, and including practices after the experience that cannot have shaped it.

Self-selected from psychedelic communities; requiring two or more uses excludes people who stopped after a difficult first experience (survivor bias, acknowledged), which bears directly on the first-experience correlations; many excluded on attention checks, with numbers only in the supplement.

Practices after the experience (a rest day, talking with someone, creative and mindful pursuits) and later meaning-making, which the authors suggest may change memories of the experience, could alter how it was rated.
Exclusions and non-response reported only in the supplement; two CEQ items missing for everyone; one practice without importance scores.
CEQ and EBI rated retrospectively, years later for most first experiences, in the same sitting as the practice checklist and by the same person; CEQ short of 2 of its 26 items.

Pre-registered hypotheses and labelled exploratory analyses, but practice-level data only in an image and the supplement, four of the possible post hoc contrasts reported, and the registration not read for this card.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence that harm-reduction practices make psychedelic experiences better or less difficult, the correlations are at very high risk of bias: nothing was adjusted, the score is weighted by the same respondents' importance judgments and includes practices after the experience, everything was recalled at one sitting (for first experiences, years later), and people who stopped after a difficult first experience could not take part. The qualitative part is a reasonable catalogue of views from 61 comments, with two authors coding, but no reflexivity or saturation account, and it describes beliefs, not effects. Cite the paper for what this self-selected group of experienced people recalled and how they rated practices (for example, being with trusted friends common and rated important; an unintoxicated sitter uncommon and rated low; testing rated important but seldom done), for the shift in place and intention between first and recent experiences, and, as hypothesis-generating, for weak correlations of a weighted practice score with emotional breakthrough (r = 0.24) and, for first experiences only, with fewer challenging experiences (r = −0.21). Do not cite it for any practice preventing challenging experiences, for harm reduction increasing with experience as a measured change, or for party settings causing worse experiences.

key_findings.finding: 163 participants after exclusions, recruited through university societies and online psychedelic communities: mean age 27.5 (SD 8.06), median 26, mode 20, range 18 to 56, 13 aged 40 or over; 120 men, 35 women, 8 non-binary. Estimated lifetime psychedelic uses: mean 28.4 (SD 45.2), median 11.5, mode 20; 16 people estimated 100 to 300 uses.
key_findings.locator: Results › Participant characteristics and psychedelic use history, 1st paragraph; Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: In the PMC rendering the mode and median age and the mode number of uses are typeset as citation links to references 20 and 26 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Time since the first experience: mean 67.52 months (SD 78.33), median 42, mode 24; since the most recent: mean 8.68 months (SD 20.76), median 2, mode 1. Substance, first and most recent: LSD 47% and 33%, psilocybin 41% and 36%, 2C-B 4% and 6%, DMT 2% and 6%, mescaline 1% and 1%, other 6% and 18%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, time and drug rows; Results › Characteristics of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Place of the first and the most recent experience: at home (including temporary residences such as hotels, holiday cottages and student dormitories) 41% and 57%; a trusted friend's house 31% and 18%; in nature 11% and 12%; a festival 7% and 4%; a club 5% and 5%; a ceremonial setting 0% and 2%; a house or outdoor party 3% and 0%; at school 1% and 0%; unclear 1% and 2%. Where two places were given, the first was counted.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, location rows and footnote; Results › Characteristics of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Intentions (more than one allowed), first and most recent experience: curiosity 72% and 20%; fun 66% and 57%; spiritual pursuits 20% and 46%; self-enlightenment 19% and 41%; exploring therapeutic properties 15% and 37%; processing difficult emotions 9% and 32%; artistic inspiration 9% and 25%; no intention 4% and 1%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, intention rows; Results › Characteristics of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Participant Harm Reduction Score (sum of the sample-mean importance of the practices used): first experience 40.06 (SD 18.90), most recent 48.68 (18.81); repeated-measures ANOVA, main effect of occasion F(1,162) = 28.32, p < 0.001; occasion by time interaction significant; Bonferroni contrasts higher for the most recent experience for practices before use (t = −9.63, p < 0.001) and after use (t = −3.28, p = 0.03), not during use (t = −1.47, p = 1) or for the during-myths (t = −0.04, p = 1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Harm reduction practices used during first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, Harm Reduction Score row
key_findings.note: The printed effect sizes and one df in this paragraph are inconsistent (see reporting issues); cite F(1,162) = 28.32 with the means.

key_findings.finding: Experience scores: EBI first 27.77 (SD 26.46), most recent 39.18 (29.91), paired t(162) = 4.42, p < 0.001, d = 0.35; CEQ (percent of maximum) first 17.14 (18.06), most recent 17.29 (17.06), with no meaningful difference in any of the seven subscales. EBI and CEQ were positively correlated (exploratory): r = 0.393 (first) and 0.369 (most recent), both p < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 2, EBI and CEQ rows

key_findings.finding: Pre-registered associations: the Participant Harm Reduction Score correlated with EBI at r = 0.24 (p = 0.002) for both experiences and with CEQ at r = −0.21 (p = 0.006) for the first experience; for the most recent experience the CEQ correlation was r = −0.15 (p = 0.061). Editors' 95% intervals (Fisher z, n = 163): 0.09 to 0.38; −0.35 to −0.06; −0.30 to 0.00.
key_findings.locator: Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Unplanned descriptive comparison, no tests: first experience in a party, club or festival setting (n = 24) versus elsewhere (n = 139): practice score 21.95 (SD 12.61) vs 43.20 (18.57), CEQ 19.27 (18.02) vs 16.77 (18.10), with the difference mainly in the isolation subscale (29.44 vs 17.36), EBI 20.38 (24.16) vs 29.05 (26.71). Most recent experience, party (n = 12) versus elsewhere (n = 151): practice score 26.23 (12.25) vs 50.46 (18.10), CEQ 31.46 (24.02) vs 16.16 (15.96), all subscales numerically higher, EBI 41.56 (23.56) vs 39.00 (30.31).
key_findings.locator: Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Table 1 implies 14, not 12, most recent experiences at a festival or club (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Individual practices as described in the text: ensuring one was comfortable with one's surroundings had the highest importance score of all practices and was reported more often for the most recent experience; most participants were with trusted friends on both occasions (high score), while few had an unintoxicated trip sitter (low score); few tested their drugs although testing scored high, while many obtained drugs from a reputable source, especially for the most recent experience; most allowed a rest day and spoke to someone afterwards, the two highest-scoring after-use practices; about 35% reported being in a dark room, a practice scored close to zero. Practices reported more often for the most recent experience also included setting a purpose, measuring the dose and arranging a time to take the drug.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Results › Theme 2 Importance of the drug, 2nd paragraph; Subtheme 3.2 Darkness versus light, 1st paragraph; Subtheme 3.3 Tripping alone versus in company, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Percentages and scores for each practice are only in Figure 1 (an image that came back blank on screenshot because the browser pane was hidden; figure image not viewable) and supplementary Table S3 (not read).

key_findings.finding: More than 70% of participants, for both the first and the most recent experience, reported at least one of the practices the authors classed as myths; relatively many reported smoking cannabis, isolating themselves from others to focus on negative thoughts and problems, and being in a dark room, the last two being practices that harm-reduction websites suggest only for more experienced people.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths, limitations and future directions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Qualitative analysis (61 free-text comments; three themes): (1) profound positive experiences, with comments that the survey missed benefits and that not every hard trip is a bad one; (2) the importance of the drug: practices depend on the substance, some comments voiced substance-specific beliefs that the authors say are not, to their knowledge, evidence-based (about cannabis with LSD as against psilocybin, and about eating or fasting before particular substances), testing was seen as important for pills or powders from unknown sources and less so for mushrooms, especially home-grown, a trusted source was seen as making testing unnecessary, and the amount taken was described as among the most important safety factors; (3) set and setting, which participants described largely as creating safe, calm spaces and reducing stress and anxiety.
key_findings.locator: Results › Qualitative analysis of free-text responses, 1st paragraph; Theme 1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Theme 2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Theme 3, 1st paragraph (block quotations not counted as paragraphs)

key_findings.finding: Qualitative subthemes on set and setting: many participants said their set-and-setting practices aimed to improve the experience rather than to make it safer, and distinguished practices that reduce harm from those that improve the experience; they proposed adding being in a good mood beforehand, clearing the mind through meditation or mindfulness, having no commitments that day and limiting phone and social media use before and during the experience; the effect of darkness was said to depend on other circumstances (frightening when alone, disorienting at a club); participants were ambivalent about using alone and about sober sitters (a sober person without psychedelic experience may make communication harder), preferred companions who are deeply trusted or experienced, and thought a support person matters more for first-time use than later.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subtheme 3.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Subtheme 3.2, 1st paragraph; Subtheme 3.3, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph (block quotations not counted as paragraphs)

key_findings.finding: Measurement problems stated by the authors: 2 of the 3 CEQ insanity items were not asked (experimenter error), so that subscale had one item; one practice (arranging a time to take the dose) had no importance scores (methodological error).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measures › Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ), 1st paragraph; Harm reduction practices, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: a self-selected, largely male sample from psychedelic forums and organizations, with possible survivor bias; many exclusions on attention checks; recall and forgetting, especially for the first experience and for practices before and after it, with post-trip meaning-making possibly changing memories; CEQ and EBI used as proxies for negative and positive experiences; the missing CEQ items; and an underpowered, exploratory setting analysis.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths, limitations and future directions, 2nd to 5th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The ANOVA paragraph is garbled: the main effect of occasion, F(1,162) = 28.32, is printed with partial eta squared 0.012, while F and df give 0.15 (editors' calculation); the same sentence then attaches F(3,486) = 563.82, partial eta squared 0.78, the values of a three-df effect (apparently the main effect of time, which the authors call not meaningful), to the statement that scores were higher for the most recent experience.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Harm reduction practices used during first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither printed effect size can be cited for the occasion effect; cite F(1,162) = 28.32, p < 0.001 with the means from Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The occasion by time interaction is printed as F(3,162) = 24.76 with partial eta squared 0.133; in a 4 × 2 within-person design with 163 people the error df is 486, and 0.133 is what F = 24.76 gives with (3, 486); with (3, 162) it would be 0.31 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Harm reduction practices used during first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Misprinted df; the effect size matches (3, 486). No change to the conclusion.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 counts 14 most recent experiences at a festival (6) or a club (8) and none at a house or outdoor party, but the party-setting group for the most recent experience in Table 2 has 12 (the Table 2 subgroup means reproduce the overall means with 12 and 151, editors' check); for the first experience the 24 in Table 2 matches Table 1 (festival 11, club 8, house party 3, outdoor party 2).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 location rows; Table 2 column headings
reporting_issues.consequence: Two most recent experiences are classified differently in the two tables without explanation; the descriptive party comparison for the most recent experience rests on 12 people either way and cannot support a claim about party settings.

reporting_issues.issue: The limitations paragraph says that use in party settings was associated with higher CEQ and lower EBI scores, but no tests were run, and Table 2 and the Results text show lower EBI in party settings for the first experience only (most recent: 41.56 versus 39.00).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Strengths, limitations and future directions, 5th paragraph; Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Table 2, not the limitations sentence; the EBI pattern by setting is inconsistent across occasions.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the practices were negatively associated with CEQ scores particularly for the first experience; the Results show no statistically significant association for the most recent experience (r = −0.15, p = 0.061), while the EBI correlation was identical on both occasions (r = 0.24).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Any claim about fewer challenging experiences should be limited to the first experience and to a weak correlation.

reporting_issues.issue: In the PMC text the mode age (20), the median age (26) and the mode number of lifetime uses (20) are typeset as citation links to references 20 and 26.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Participant characteristics and psychedelic use history, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the mode age of 20 is confirmed in the next subsection, and the values can be read as data.
